label: Chapter 3: Capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, 1430 to 1568

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In 1430, Brussels hits the jackpot.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It really does. The duchy of Brabant passes to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, one of the richest and most glamorous princes in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Philip makes a choice that changes the city's destiny.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Out of all his great towns, he picks Brussels as his main residence.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, I have to ask. What was the Burgundian state?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Because it sounds like a wine region.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ha. Not quite. It wasn't a kingdom on a map the way we think of kingdoms.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a patchwork of territories collected through marriage, inheritance, and purchase.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Flanders, Brabant, Holland, Hainaut, and soon the duchy of Luxembourg, which Philip took in 1443, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So roughly modern Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Plus a good slice of northern France.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Philip ruled it all from the most dazzling court in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Knights, painters, musicians, diplomats.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1430, the same year he inherited Brabant, he founded a famous chivalric brotherhood, the Order of the Golden Fleece.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Every club needs a good name. And the heart of that court was Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More and more. The dukes lived at the Coudenberg Palace, on the hill above the town, and enlarged it into a huge complex of halls, chapels, and courtyards.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Government offices followed the court.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Money followed the offices.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And artists followed the money.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Artists always follow the money.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So let's talk art, because this is a golden age.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's extraordinary. In 1436, the city appoints a painter named Rogier van der Weyden as its official city painter.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He was born in Tournai, trained there, and became one of the great masters of what we now call Early Netherlandish painting.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: His portraits have those sharp, searching faces.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Like they know what you did.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And emotional religious scenes, admired across Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the town hall, he painted a series of panels about justice, scenes of rulers hearing the cases of ordinary people.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Can we go and see them?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No. They were destroyed in 1695.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We'll get to that.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Of course we will.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The artist's reputation lived on, though.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Rogier is buried in the cathedral of Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then there's tapestry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels becomes famous for it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Weavers in the city produce huge, richly colored wall hangings, made of wool, silk, and threads of gold and silver.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Tapestries were the luxury art of the age.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A prince would pay more for a fine set than for a painting.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait, more than a painting? For a rug on the wall?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For a very, very good rug on the wall.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they could be rolled up and carried from palace to palace.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a portable fortune.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, that makes sense. And I remember a Sistine Chapel connection.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the second decade of the sixteenth century, Pope Leo the Tenth commissions a set of tapestries for the Sistine Chapel, from designs by Raphael.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the weaving is done in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city soon introduces a quality mark, a pair of the letter B around a red shield, woven into the edge of authentic pieces to protect the brand.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A brand mark. In the fifteen hundreds.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's very modern.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very. But the Burgundian dream ends abruptly in 1477.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip's grandson, Charles the Bold, is killed fighting the Swiss and the Lorrainers outside the city of Nancy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he leaves a single daughter, Mary of Burgundy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who was born in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And she's the most eligible heiress in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She marries Maximilian of Habsburg, an Austrian prince who will become Holy Roman Emperor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And when she dies in a riding accident in 1482, her lands pass to their children.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Through that marriage, the Burgundian Netherlands falls into the hands of the Habsburgs, the most powerful dynasty of the next three centuries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Habsburg who matters most for Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Mary's grandson, Charles. He's born in Ghent in the year 1500, but he's raised in the Netherlands, and he sees Brussels as home.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When he's six, he inherits the Burgundian lands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1516, he's proclaimed King of Spain, in a ceremony in the church of Saint Gudula in Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait. King of Spain. In Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In Brussels. And in 1519, he's elected Holy Roman Emperor, as Charles the Fifth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So a boy from Ghent, raised in the Netherlands, ends up ruling an enormous empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From Spain and Italy to Germany, the Netherlands, and the new Spanish colonies in the Americas.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: He can't have been in Brussels very often.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He was usually traveling, so he needed trusted regents to govern the Netherlands in his absence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His aunt Margaret of Austria ruled from nearby Mechelen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Later, his sister Mary of Hungary took over.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1531, the central government institutions are fixed in Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So that's the moment it becomes the capital of the Low Countries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A role it has kept, in one form or another, ever since.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it's a brilliant time intellectually, isn't it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. In 1521, the great humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam, the most famous scholar in Europe, spends several months in Anderlecht, then a village outside Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In a house you can visit today as a museum.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Vesalius was a Brussels boy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Andreas Vesalius, born in Brussels in 1514.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He grows up to be a pioneer of modern anatomy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His groundbreaking book on the structure of the human body, published in 1543, corrected centuries of errors by examining real corpses.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which I imagine did not go down well at dinner parties.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It went down very well in the history of medicine.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Bruegel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1563, Pieter Bruegel the Elder moves to Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He marries the daughter of a well-known local artist, and in the remaining years of his short life, he paints some of his most famous scenes of peasant life and village feasts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He dies in Brussels in 1569, and he's buried in a church in the Marolles district.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Charles left another mark on the city, didn't he?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A festival.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1549, there's a great festival in Brussels to present his son and heir, Philip, to the people of the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The procession of guilds, nobles, and giant figures that winds through the streets is remembered today in a summer pageant called the Ommegang, held every year on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Giant figures. I'm in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a good one.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then the abdication. That's such a scene.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. In October of 1555, in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace, Charles gives up his crown.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exhausted, ill, and weary of ruling, he announces he's handing the Netherlands over to Philip the Second.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Witnesses record that he leaned on the shoulder of a young nobleman, the twenty-two-year-old William of Orange, and that the hall wept as he spoke.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then he retired to a monastery.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Soon afterward he handed Spain over too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And yes, a monastery.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The most dramatic retirement in history.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: "I'm tired. Here is most of the world."

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Take it, I'm going to lie down.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the picture isn't all golden, is it?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Reformation arrives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By now Brussels is a city of tens of thousands of people, a great center of government, art, and trade.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But dark clouds are on the horizon.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther challenged the Catholic Church, and the new Protestant ideas spread quickly through the Low Countries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the authorities reacted.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did. And this part is not funny.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1523, in the very center of Brussels, two young Augustinian monks, Henry Voes and Johannes van den Esschen, were burned at the stake on the Grand Place for refusing to renounce Luther's teachings.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right here. In the square we've been joking about.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the same square. They're considered the first martyrs of the Protestant Reformation.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a sign of things to come.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the new ruler?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip the Second is a devoutly Catholic king who lives in Spain and never really understands the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He intends to stamp out heresy, enforce Catholic orthodoxy, and tighten royal control over the proud cities.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the cities, with their ancient privileges, weren't going to take that lying down.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not without a fight.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. If someone wants to touch this chapter, where do they go?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Place Royale, at the top of the hill.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Under the square, an archaeological site called the Coudenberg lets you walk through the surviving cellars and streets of the old ducal palace.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll be standing on the same ground where Charles the Fifth gave up the biggest empire in the world.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Stubbornness tally?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip the Second against every city in the Netherlands?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I think we're about to jump.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next time, revolt, execution, bombardment, and an elegant rebuilding.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A busy century and a half.
